subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - Water and Food Security
subtitle: How geography, climate, population, resources, and choices affect reliable access to water and food.
description: This pack helps students revise why safe water and nutritious food are unevenly available across the world. It connects physical geography, human geography, real-world case studies, map skills, climate data, sustainability, and common misconceptions about water and food security.

data.targetWord: an area of Earth with shared features, such as climate, culture, landforms, or economy

examples.en-US: Region helps geographers compare places with similar or different features.

data.targetWord: the natural and human-made surroundings where people, plants, and animals live

examples.en-US: The environment includes rivers, farms, roads, homes, soils, and ecosystems.

data.targetWord: how crowded an area is, usually measured as people per square mile or square kilometer

data.targetWord: reliable access to enough safe, nutritious, and affordable food for an active and healthy life

data.targetWord: supplying water to crops using canals, pipes, sprinklers, or other systems

examples.en-US: Overuse of groundwater can make wells deeper and more expensive.

data.title: How Drought Can Lead to Food Insecurity
data.instruction: Put the drought-to-food-insecurity chain in order.
items: Rainfall is much lower than usual.
River flow decreases and soil becomes very dry.
Crops grow poorly and livestock have less pasture or water.
Harvests decrease.
Food prices rise.
Low-income families buy less food or less nutritious food.
Malnutrition risk increases and migration, aid, or adaptation may occur.

data.title: The Water Cycle and Human Use
data.instruction: Put the water movement steps in a logical order.
items: Water evaporates from oceans, lakes, rivers, and soils.
Water vapor cools and condenses into clouds.
Precipitation falls as rain or snow.
Some water runs off into rivers and lakes.
Some water infiltrates into soil and groundwater.
Plants take up water and release some through transpiration.
Water returns to rivers, lakes, oceans, and the air.

data.title: Two-Year Drought Event Timeline
data.instruction: Put the fictional drought events in the order given in the study pack.
items: Winter rainfall is below average, so reservoirs do not refill fully.
Farmers plant crops using stored water, increasing irrigation demand.
A summer heat wave increases evaporation and dries soils faster.
The fall harvest is smaller than usual and local food prices rise.
Drought continues into the next winter and groundwater pumping increases.
Some wells run low and families travel farther for water.
Outdoor water use is limited and aid programs or crop changes begin.

data.title: Using Map Evidence Like a Geographer
data.instruction: Put these map interpretation steps in a sensible order.
items: Identify the area shown on the map.
Check what the colors, labels, and symbols mean.
Find the highest and lowest values or most important places.
Describe the main spatial pattern.
Suggest physical and human reasons for the pattern.
Ask what information is missing before making a final judgement.
